transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I can’t stop fixating on how awful I look on camera and in photos, and it’s starting to affect my work and social life. It has gotten to the point where I'm avoiding important parts of my job and staying home from social outings, which is why a close friend urged me to come speak with you.
Besides worries about how you look, do you also spend a lot of time feeling down or tense about many different things in life, or is the main problem specifically your appearance?

No, I don't really feel anxious or down about other things in my life; the main problem is specifically how I look. All of my stress and avoidance are tied directly to seeing my dark circles, eye bags, and how bloated and uneven my face looks on screen. When I'm not focused on that, I'm generally fine, but this one thing has just completely taken over.
Do you avoid social situations mainly because you fear other people will judge your appearance, or is the concern mostly about your own distress when you see yourself in photos or on camera?

It’s really a combination of both. I feel incredibly distressed when I see my dark circles and bloated face on camera, and I'll replay those images in my head for hours afterward. But I also worry constantly that everyone else is judging me and thinking I look exhausted and sloppy, which makes any social outing where photos might be taken feel like a total minefield.
Do you think there is a real defect or flaw in your appearance that others would also notice, or do you mainly worry about being judged or embarrassed in social situations?

I absolutely believe it is a real physical defect, as my dark circles and bloated, uneven face are incredibly obvious to me. I am convinced that others are noticing these flaws and thinking I look exhausted and sloppy, even though my friends and coworkers claim they don't see anything wrong. It feels like a very real, visible problem rather than just a general worry about being judged.

When you avoid social situations, is it mainly because you fear people will judge or embarrass you in general, or because you are preoccupied with the specific appearance flaw itself even when no one else seems to notice it?

It’s definitely because I am so preoccupied with these specific flaws, like my eye bags and bloated face, rather than a general fear of social situations. I am just so consumed by how awful I look that I'd rather skip an event entirely than risk being photographed, even if my friends tell me they don't notice anything.
How much time each day do you spend thinking about or checking these appearance concerns, and do you do things like mirror checking, comparing photos, or seeking reassurance because of them?

I spend hours every day fixating on this, often replaying images of my face in my head for hours. Before any video meeting or event, I spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting the lighting, angles, and my makeup to hide my puffy face. During and after calls, I constantly check my camera box, zoom in on flaws in tagged photos, and ask my friends for reassurance that I didn't look terrible.

When you avoid social or work situations, is it mainly because you fear being embarrassed or judged in general, or because you are preoccupied with a specific flaw in your appearance even when other people say they do not notice it?

My avoidance is entirely because of my preoccupation with my dark circles and puffy face, not a general fear of embarrassment. Even though my coworkers and friends say they don't notice anything, I'm convinced I look bloated and exhausted on camera, which makes me want to hide and avoid being seen or photographed at all.

Do you avoid social or work situations mainly because you fear being judged or embarrassed by other people in general, or is it mostly because of a specific concern about your appearance even when others say they do not notice a problem?

It is definitely the latter, as my avoidance is entirely driven by my obsession with how my face looks, specifically my dark circles and bloated appearance. Even when my friends and colleagues reassure me that they don't notice anything wrong, I still can't stop fixating on these flaws. That is why I avoid these situations, rather than having a general fear of people.

Have you ever felt that the problem is more about being judged or embarrassed in social situations in general, even when your appearance is not the focus, or is it only about the specific flaw in your appearance?

No, it is strictly about the specific flaws in my appearance, like my bloated face and dark circles. I actually don't have a general fear of social situations at all—I used to be very active with dancing and soccer, and I only started skipping those outings because I'm terrified of being photographed or tagged on social media.

Do you ever worry that you have a serious medical or physical illness because of these appearance concerns, or is the problem mainly that you think your appearance is flawed and others will notice it?

No, I don't worry about having a medical illness; the issue is purely aesthetic. I am just deeply self-conscious about looking bloated and uneven with these dark circles, and I constantly worry that others will notice and judge me for looking exhausted and sloppy.
Do you ever avoid social situations because you feel awkward or afraid of being judged even when your appearance is not the focus, or is it only because of the specific flaws you see in your face?

No, I don't feel awkward or anxious in social situations for any other reason; it is strictly because of how I look. I only avoid these events because I am terrified of people seeing my bloated face and dark circles, or being captured in an unflattering photo.

When you avoid events, is it mainly because you fear being embarrassed or judged in social situations in general, or is it almost entirely because you are preoccupied with the specific appearance flaws you see in your face?

It is almost entirely because of my preoccupation with my specific flaws, like my dark circles and bloated, uneven face, and the dread of being captured on camera. I don't have a general fear of social situations at all. I just can't bear the thought of people seeing or photographing these parts of my face.
Do you ever think there is a chance your concern about your appearance might be exaggerated or not actually visible to others, or are you completely certain that the flaw is real and obvious?

Even though my friends and coworkers tell me they don't notice anything wrong, I am completely convinced that the dark circles and the bloated, uneven look of my face are very real and highly visible. I just can't help but feel that everyone is secretly judging me and thinking I look exhausted and sloppy.

Do you also have a strong fear of being embarrassed or judged in social situations even when your appearance is not being noticed, or is your distress only about the specific flaw you see in your appearance?

No, my distress is strictly about the specific flaws in my appearance. I don't have a general fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations at all. My anxiety and avoidance, like skipping soccer or parties, are purely driven by the fear of being photographed or having others notice my dark circles and bloated face.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying that you have a serious illness or disease because of these symptoms, or is your concern mainly that your appearance looks flawed or unattractive?

No, I don't worry about having a medical illness or disease at all. My concern is entirely that my appearance looks flawed, bloated, and uneven, which makes me look incredibly unattractive and exhausted on camera. I am just deeply distressed by how I look in photos, not by any fear of being sick.

Do you ever think there is even a small chance that your concern about your face may be exaggerated or not as visible to others as it feels to you, or are you completely certain the flaw is real and obvious?

Even though my friends and coworkers tell me they don't notice anything wrong, I am completely convinced that my bloated face and dark circles are real and highly obvious. When I look in the mirror or on camera, it feels absolutely undeniable, and I often worry that others are just trying to be nice when they say they don't see it.

Do you ever think there is a chance that your concern about your appearance might be exaggerated or not actually visible to other people, or are you completely certain that the flaw is real and obvious?

Even though others tell me they don't notice anything wrong, I am completely convinced that my dark circles and bloated face are real and highly obvious. I constantly replay those images in my head, certain that everyone thinks I look exhausted and sloppy, which is why I keep asking my friends for reassurance.

Have you ever believed that other people are deliberately talking about, mocking, or targeting you because of your appearance, or is your concern limited to being very distressed about how your face looks?

No, I don't think people are deliberately mocking or targeting me maliciously. I am just constantly convinced that anyone looking at me must be thinking I look exhausted, bloated, and sloppy because of my dark circles and uneven face. My distress is entirely about those specific flaws and the fear of being judged for them.
Do you think there is any chance that these appearance concerns might be exaggerated or not actually visible to other people, or are you completely certain that the flaw is real and obvious?

I am completely convinced that these flaws—specifically my dark circles and puffy, uneven face—are real and highly obvious, even if my friends and coworkers say they don't notice anything. I just can't help but feel that everyone is secretly judging me and thinking I look exhausted and sloppy when they see me.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with body dysmorphic disorder: the patient has a persistent preoccupation with perceived facial defects (dark circles, puffy/uneven face), spends hours thinking about them, performs repetitive checking/reassurance-seeking behaviors, shows marked distress and avoidance of work/social situations, and has poor insight with near-delusional conviction that the flaw is real and obvious. Symptoms are focused on appearance rather than a broader social fear or a general illness concern.
